subject: Architecture
title: Hempcrete: Building with Plants
description: A quick win: understand Hempcrete: Building with Plants.

hook.text: Hempcrete is a building material made from hemp fibers and lime. It's lightweight, insulating, and carbon-negative.

buildup.text: Hemp grows in four months, requires no pesticides, and absorbs CO₂ as it grows.

discovery.text: Mixed with lime, hemp fibers harden into blocks that insulate, regulate moisture, and resist fire.

twist.text: Hempcrete absorbs more CO₂ over its lifetime than was emitted making it — a truly carbon-negative material.

climax.text: France has used hempcrete for decades. The material is now spreading to the U.S. and Australia.

punchline.text: A weed mixed with lime might save the construction industry.

quiz.question: Why is hempcrete considered carbon-negative?
options: It absorbs more CO₂ over its lifetime than was emitted making it
It replaces trees that would otherwise be cut down

details.summary: Hempcrete mixes hemp hurd (the woody core of the cannabis plant) with lime binder to create a lightweight insulating material that is carbon-negative — it absorbs more CO2 during the hemp's growth than is emitted during manufacturing.
details.whyItMatters: Hempcrete is one of very few building materials that is carbon-negative. As construction seeks to reduce its carbon footprint.
takeaways: Hemp hurd mixed with lime creates a carbon-negative insulation
The hemp plant absorbs more CO2 during growth than manufacturing emits
Hempcrete regulates humidity and is naturally fire-resistant

faq.question: Is hempcrete load-bearing?
faq.answer: No. Hempcrete is an insulating infill material, not a structural one. It's typically used to fill timber or steel frames, providing insulation and moisture regulation. Its compressive strength is too low for load-bearing, but it reduces the overall weight of wall assemblies significantly.

faq.question: Is hempcrete legal in the United States?
faq.answer: Yes. The 2018 Farm Bill legalized industrial hemp cultivation federally. Hempcrete is permitted in construction, though building codes for it are still developing. Several US buildings have used hempcrete, and interest is growing as the material gains building code recognition.
